region: Byzantium & Orthodox East; Latin palace and cathedral schools

institutions.name: Magnaura School
institutions.summary: Higher school set up in the Magnaura hall of the Great Palace by the Caesar Bardas, with Leo the Mathematician at its head teaching philosophy and the mathematical sciences. It was the main centre of the 9th-century Byzantine revival of classical learning and was revived by Constantine VII in the 10th century.
institutions.notes: Founding date conventional: sources give c. 849, 855/856 or 863 (Bardas was Caesar from 862). Continuity after Constantine VII is obscure; end set to the 1046 refoundation of imperial higher teaching (b-pandidakterion).

institutions.name: Pandidakterion (Imperial School of Philosophy, Constantinople)
alt: School of Philosophy of Constantine IX
institutions.summary: The imperial higher school of philosophy refounded by Constantine IX Monomachos, with Michael Psellos as 'consul of the philosophers' and John Italos as his successor. Dispersed by the Latin sack of 1204, imperial higher teaching was restored after 1261 under George Akropolites and lasted until the Ottoman conquest.
institutions.notes: This record treats imperial higher teaching in Constantinople from 1046 as one institution; the late-antique Pandidakterion of 425 lies outside the dataset range. Its continuity across 1204-1261 and in the Palaiologan period is a modelling choice; teaching was often attached to individual masters and monasteries.

institutions.name: Law School of Constantinople (Didaskaleion ton nomon)
alt: School of Law of Constantine IX
institutions.summary: State law school established by Constantine IX Monomachos at the Mangana monastery of St George, headed by John Xiphilinos with the title nomophylax. It trained judges and officials and certified those admitted to legal practice.
institutions.notes: The founding novel (Novella of Constantine IX, preserved via John Mauropous) is dated 1045 or 1047 in the literature. Its activity after the later 11th century is poorly documented; end set at 1204.

institutions.name: Patriarchal Academy of Constantinople
institutions.summary: Higher school of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, organized in the 12th century around the 'teachers' of Hagia Sophia and re-established after 1453 by Patriarch Gennadios Scholarios. As the 'Great School of the Nation' it was the principal school of the Greek Orthodox world under Ottoman rule.
institutions.notes: Tradition traces a patriarchal school to late antiquity; 1107 (Alexios I's edict on the patriarchal didaskaloi) is used as a conventional start. Refoundation date 1454 is traditional (Wikipedia's infobox gives 1597). Seat after 1454 varied (Phanar from c. 1601); moved to Xirokrini in 1804; present Phanar building 1881-83.

institutions.name: Imperial court schools of Nicaea
institutions.summary: Higher teaching sustained by the Laskarid emperors of Nicaea during the Latin occupation of Constantinople, notably by Nikephoros Blemmydes. It preserved Byzantine learning and trained the officials who restored the empire in 1261.
institutions.notes: Teaching was dispersed among court, monasteries and individual masters (Blemmydes taught near Ephesus); Theodore II Laskaris founded schools at Nicaea in the 1250s. Treated as one record for mapping.

institutions.name: Chora Monastery school and library
institutions.summary: The Chora monastery restored by the statesman Theodore Metochites, who endowed it with one of the great libraries of late Byzantium. Under Metochites and his pupil Nikephoros Gregoras it was a centre of astronomy and humanist scholarship.
institutions.notes: Not a formal school; included as a centre of higher study. Restoration 1316-1321 approx.

institutions.name: School of Plethon at Mistra
institutions.summary: Circle of pupils gathered around the Neoplatonist philosopher George Gemistos Plethon at the court of the Despots of the Morea. Its pupils, above all Bessarion, carried Platonism to Italy.
institutions.notes: Plethon's arrival at Mistra is dated c. 1407-1414. Ended with Plethon's death (1452) and the Ottoman conquest of the Morea (1460).

institutions.name: Patmian School
institutions.summary: School founded by the monk Makarios Kalogeras near the Monastery of St John on Patmos, one of the leading Greek schools of the 18th century. It drew students from across the Greek world.
institutions.notes: Periods of decline after 1800; continued as a school into the 20th century.

institutions.name: Athonite Academy
institutions.summary: Academy founded by Vatopedi monastery with the support of Patriarch Cyril V, which under Eugenios Voulgaris taught modern philosophy and mathematics alongside theology. Conservative monastic opposition forced Voulgaris out and it declined, closing in 1821; it was revived at Karyes in the 1840s.
institutions.notes: Revival date given as 1842 or 1845.

institutions.name: Gioumeios School, Ioannina
institutions.summary: Ioannina school endowed by the merchant Emmanuel Gioumas, one of the institutions that made Ioannina a leading Greek educational centre. Methodios Anthrakites studied and later taught there; it was afterwards associated with the conservative Balanos family.
institutions.notes: Founding date c. 1676 conventional; end approximate (Ali Pasha's fall, 1820-22).

institutions.name: Maroutsaia School, Ioannina
institutions.summary: School founded with funds from the Maroutsis merchant family of Venice, where Eugenios Voulgaris first taught modern philosophy and experimental physics. It was a key early institution of the Modern Greek Enlightenment.

institutions.name: Kaplaneios School, Ioannina
institutions.summary: School endowed by the brothers Zois and Manthos Kaplanis and directed by Athanasios Psalidas, who taught natural science and modern philosophy. It was destroyed in the fighting around Ali Pasha's fall.

institutions.name: Evangelical School of Smyrna
institutions.summary: Greek school of Smyrna founded by the Orthodox community and placed under British consular protection in 1747. It became one of the most important Greek educational institutions of Asia Minor, with a noted library and museum.
institutions.notes: Destroyed in 1922 (outside range).

institutions.name: School of Chios
institutions.summary: Community higher school of Chios, directed by Athanasios Parios and later reorganized on Enlightenment lines by Neophytos Vamvas, with a library, laboratory and printing press. At its height it had several hundred students; it was destroyed in the Chios massacre.
institutions.notes: An older community school existed; 1788 (Parios' directorship) used as start. Reorganized 1792 and again under Vamvas from 1815.

institutions.name: Academy of Kydonies
institutions.summary: Greek academy of the self-governing town of Kydonies, which under Benjamin of Lesbos and Theophilos Kairis taught mathematics, physics and philosophy to hundreds of students. It was destroyed when Ottoman forces burned the town in 1821.
institutions.notes: Founding variously 1798-1803.

institutions.name: Ionian Academy
institutions.summary: The first modern Greek institution of higher education, founded in Corfu by the philhellene Lord Guilford under the British-protected United States of the Ionian Islands. It had faculties of theology, law, medicine and philosophy and declined after Guilford's death, being abolished after union with Greece.
institutions.notes: Guilford planned it from 1811; formal opening 1824.

institutions.name: University of Athens
alt: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
institutions.summary: The first university of the Greek state and of the Eastern Mediterranean, founded by King Otto on the German model with faculties of theology, law, medicine and philosophy. It trained the professional and intellectual elite of the Greek world.

institutions.name: Athens Polytechnic (School of Arts)
institutions.summary: Founded as a Sunday school of building crafts and soon a school of arts and engineering, it grew into Greece's polytechnic. Benefactors from Metsovo funded its Patission Street complex.
institutions.notes: Upgraded to a higher technical school in stages (1863, 1887).

institutions.name: Theological School of Halki
institutions.summary: Principal theological school of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, founded by Patriarch Germanos IV on the site of the Holy Trinity monastery on Halki. It trained much of the Orthodox hierarchy.
institutions.notes: Closed by Turkish law in 1971 (outside range).

institutions.name: Rizarios Ecclesiastical School
institutions.summary: Ecclesiastical school in Athens endowed by the Epirote brothers Manthos and Georgios Rizaris to train Orthodox clergy. It was a leading seminary of the Greek kingdom.

institutions.name: Belgrade Higher School (1808)
institutions.summary: Higher school founded in revolutionary Serbia by Ivan Jugović with Dositej Obradović's support, teaching law, history, mathematics and languages. It closed when the Ottomans reconquered Serbia in 1813.

institutions.name: Lyceum and Higher School of Belgrade
institutions.summary: Founded as the Lyceum of the Principality of Serbia in Kragujevac, moved to Belgrade, and reorganized in 1863 as the Velika škola with faculties of philosophy, law and engineering. It became the University of Belgrade in 1905.
institutions.notes: University title only from 1905 (outside range); typed university as a multi-faculty higher school on the university model.

institutions.name: Sofia Higher School
institutions.summary: Founded as a higher pedagogical course and soon the Higher School of the Principality of Bulgaria, it became the University of Sofia in 1904. It was the first Bulgarian institution of higher education.

institutions.name: Robert College
institutions.summary: American college founded by Cyrus Hamlin and Christopher Robert, the oldest American school abroad. It educated much of the first Bulgarian political elite.

institutions.name: Syrian Protestant College
institutions.summary: College founded by American Protestant missionaries under Daniel Bliss and chartered in New York, with a medical school from 1867. Instruction was in Arabic until 1882, then English.
institutions.notes: Founded by Americans; included as a Western Christian foundation in the map extent.

institutions.name: Université Saint-Joseph
institutions.summary: Jesuit college transferred from Ghazir to Beirut, granted pontifical degree powers by Leo XIII. A French faculty of medicine was added in 1883.

institutions.name: Coptic Clerical College
institutions.summary: Theological college of the Coptic Orthodox Church founded under Pope Cyril V to train clergy. It is included as the only significant Christian higher school in Egypt before 1900.
institutions.notes: Oriental (not Byzantine) Orthodox; inclusion marginal.

institutions.name: Palace School of Charlemagne
institutions.summary: School of the Carolingian court, gathered by Charlemagne around Alcuin of York and other foreign scholars, and the engine of the Carolingian Renaissance. It educated the royal family and court nobility and set standards for script, Latin and liturgy across the empire.
institutions.notes: The court was itinerant until Aachen became its main seat c. 794; Alcuin joined in 781/782. End conventional (death of Louis the Pious, 840).

institutions.name: Palace School of Charles the Bald
institutions.summary: The court school of Charles the Bald, celebrated for the Irish master John Scottus Eriugena. It was a centre of Greek studies and theological controversy.
institutions.notes: Court was itinerant (Compiègne, Laon, Quierzy); Compiègne used for mapping.

institutions.name: Court School of Alfred the Great
institutions.summary: Circle of scholars assembled by Alfred to restore learning after the Viking wars, including Asser, Grimbald and Plegmund. It produced Old English translations of key Latin works and taught noble youths to read.
institutions.notes: Alfred's court was itinerant; Winchester conventional.

institutions.name: Ottonian Court School
institutions.summary: Court school of Otto I directed by his brother Bruno, later archbishop of Cologne. It trained the bishops of the Ottonian imperial church.
institutions.notes: Itinerant court; Aachen used for mapping.

institutions.name: Law School of Pavia
institutions.summary: School of Lombard law associated with the royal palace court of Pavia, which produced the Liber Papiensis and its commentary (Expositio). Lanfranc studied there.
institutions.notes: Dates conventional.

institutions.name: Law School of Ravenna
institutions.summary: School of Roman law at Ravenna, traditionally the predecessor of Bologna. Peter Crassus' defence of Henry IV (1084) came from it.
institutions.notes: Dates conventional.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Saint-Martin, Tours
institutions.summary: The abbey school of St Martin where Alcuin, appointed abbot in 796, trained a generation of Carolingian scholars including Hrabanus Maurus. Its scriptorium developed Caroline minuscule book production; in the 11th century the cathedral/abbey schools of Tours were made famous by Berengar's dialectic.
institutions.notes: Berengar taught at the school of Saint-Martin c. 1040-1088; end conventional.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Fulda
institutions.summary: School of the abbey founded by Sturm for St Boniface, which under Hrabanus Maurus (master from c. 804, abbot 822-842) became the foremost school of East Francia. Its pupils included Walafrid Strabo, Lupus of Ferrières and Gottschalk.
institutions.notes: School activity attested from the late 8th century; end conventional.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Reichenau
institutions.summary: Island abbey on Lake Constance founded by Pirmin, whose school, library and scriptorium were among the greatest of the Carolingian and Ottonian eras. Walafrid Strabo was abbot and Hermann the Lame taught mathematics and music there.

institutions.name: Abbey School of St Gall
institutions.summary: Benedictine abbey whose inner (monastic) and outer schools, shown on the 9th-century Plan of St Gall, made it a leading centre of learning. Notker Balbulus, Ratpert, Tuotilo, Ekkehard I and Notker Labeo taught there.
institutions.notes: Abbey library survives to the present; the school's high period ends c. 1100.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Corbie
institutions.summary: Royal abbey on the Somme with one of the great Carolingian scriptoria and libraries. Paschasius Radbertus and Ratramnus taught there, and Ansgar, apostle of the North, was educated there.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Corvey
institutions.summary: Saxon daughter house of Corbie and the leading school of 9th-10th-century Saxony. Widukind of Corvey wrote his Saxon history there.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Ferrières
institutions.summary: Abbey school that under Lupus of Ferrières (abbot 840-862) was the outstanding centre of classical text-collection in the 9th century. Heiric of Auxerre studied there.
institutions.notes: Abbey older; start = Lupus's abbacy.

institutions.name: School of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre
institutions.summary: Abbey school that produced the commentary tradition of Haimo, Heiric and Remigius of Auxerre, widely used in medieval schools. Remigius later taught at Reims and Paris.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Lyon
institutions.summary: Cathedral school restored by Archbishop Leidrad at Charlemagne's request, later the base of Agobard and the deacon Florus. It was a centre of patristic learning and of opposition to Eriugena.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Orléans
institutions.summary: Schools organized by Bishop Theodulf, whose capitulary required parish schools; in the 12th century Orléans became the foremost centre of classical authors. The schools later developed into the law university of Orléans.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Reims
institutions.summary: Cathedral school restored by Archbishop Fulk with Remigius of Auxerre and Hucbald. Under Gerbert of Aurillac (scholasticus c. 972-982) it became the most celebrated school in Europe; Bruno of Cologne, founder of the Carthusians, later taught there.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Fleury
institutions.summary: Loire abbey reformed by Odo of Cluny, whose school and library flourished under Abbo of Fleury. It supplied masters to English reformed houses such as Ramsey.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Chartres
institutions.summary: Cathedral school raised to fame by Fulbert (bishop 1006-1028) and in the 12th century by Bernard, Thierry and Gilbert of Poitiers, associated with Platonism and the liberal arts. John of Salisbury was its bishop (1176-1180).
institutions.notes: Whether a distinctive 'School of Chartres' existed in the 12th century is debated (R. W. Southern).

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Laon
institutions.summary: Cathedral school with Irish masters such as Martin Hiberniensis in the 9th century; under Anselm of Laon and his brother Ralph (c. 1080-1117) it was the leading school of biblical theology and the source of the Glossa ordinaria.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Notre-Dame, Paris
institutions.summary: Cathedral school on the Île de la Cité where William of Champeaux, Abelard and Peter Lombard taught. Its chancellor's licence to teach became a key element in the formation of the University of Paris.

institutions.name: School of Saint-Victor
institutions.summary: School of the Augustinian canons founded when William of Champeaux withdrew to St Victor. Hugh, Richard and Andrew of St Victor made it a centre of mystical theology and biblical exegesis.

institutions.name: Schools of Sainte-Geneviève
institutions.summary: Schools on the hill of Sainte-Geneviève, under the abbey's jurisdiction, where Abelard taught dialectic to large audiences. The abbey's chancellor also licensed masters on the Left Bank.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Bec
institutions.summary: Norman abbey whose external school, founded by Lanfranc, drew pupils from all over Europe. Under Anselm (prior 1063, abbot 1078) it was a centre of theology and philosophy.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Liège
institutions.summary: Cathedral school of St Lambert, where the Irish poet Sedulius Scottus worked in the 9th century; under Bishop Notger it became one of the leading schools of the empire.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Utrecht
institutions.summary: Missionary school of Gregory of Utrecht, later the cathedral school. It educated Liudger and, in the 10th century, Bruno of Cologne.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Cologne
institutions.summary: Cathedral school strengthened by Archbishop Bruno, brother of Otto I, which trained bishops for the Ottonian church.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Hildesheim
institutions.summary: Cathedral school where Bernward, later bishop and tutor of Otto III, was trained by Thangmar.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Magdeburg
institutions.summary: Cathedral school of the archdiocese founded by Otto I as a base for the Slav mission. Under Ohtrich it rivalled Reims; Adalbert of Prague and Thietmar of Merseburg studied there.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Würzburg
institutions.summary: Cathedral school of the Ottonian-Salian imperial church, noted in the 11th century for its poets and masters.
institutions.notes: Thinly documented; dates conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Bamberg
institutions.summary: Cathedral school founded with the diocese by Emperor Henry II, endowed with books from Otto III's library. It was a leading imperial school in the 11th century.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Canterbury
institutions.summary: School founded by Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian teaching Latin, Greek, computus and law. Lanfranc and Anselm later revived learning at Christ Church.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of York
institutions.summary: Cathedral school founded by Archbishop Egbert and taught by Ælbert, whose pupil Alcuin directed it before leaving for Charlemagne's court. Its library was the richest in 8th-century England.

institutions.name: Old Minster School, Winchester
institutions.summary: Monastic cathedral school of Bishop Æthelwold, a centre of the Benedictine reform and of standard Old English. Ælfric of Eynsham was trained there.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Ramsey
institutions.summary: Fenland abbey founded by Oswald, where Abbo of Fleury taught (985-987) and Byrhtferth wrote his computus manual.

institutions.name: Monastic School of Iona
institutions.summary: Columba's monastery, head of a federation of monasteries in Ireland and Britain and a centre of Latin learning (Adomnán). Viking raids forced removal of the community to Kells.

institutions.name: Monastic School of Armagh
institutions.summary: Patrician church whose school was the principal school of Ireland. The synod of Clane (1162) required Armagh's approval for all teachers of theology.

institutions.name: Monastic School of Clonmacnoise
institutions.summary: Monastery on the Shannon founded by St Ciarán, a leading Irish centre of learning and annal-writing.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Monte Cassino
institutions.summary: Benedict's foundation, where Paul the Deacon wrote and Constantine the African translated Arabic medical works under Abbot Desiderius.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Bobbio
institutions.summary: Abbey founded by Columbanus whose library was among the richest in early medieval Italy; Gerbert was its abbot in 982.

institutions.name: School of Pavia (Capitulary of Olona)
institutions.summary: Central school designated by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona, with the Irish master Dungal, for students from much of Lombardy.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Ivrea
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Ivrea. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Turin
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Turin. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Cremona
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Cremona. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Florence
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Florence. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Verona
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Verona. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Vicenza
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Vicenza. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Cividale
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Cividale. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Fermo
institutions.summary: One of the regional schools established by Lothar I's Capitulary of Olona (825) at Fermo. Later evidence of its teaching is sparse.
institutions.notes: Existence attested mainly by the capitulary; end conventional.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Vic
institutions.summary: Catalan cathedral school where Gerbert of Aurillac studied mathematics (967-970) under Bishop Atto. Catalonia transmitted Arabic mathematical learning to Latin Europe.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Ripoll
institutions.summary: Catalan abbey founded by Wilfred the Hairy whose library held early Latin works on the astrolabe and Arabic science. Oliba made it a major centre in the 11th century.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Toledo
institutions.summary: Translation centre around the cathedral of Toledo under Archbishop Raymond, where Gerard of Cremona and Dominicus Gundissalinus rendered Arabic science and philosophy into Latin.
institutions.notes: The 'school' was a milieu of translators, not a formal institution.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Santiago de Compostela
institutions.summary: Cathedral school organized by Archbishop Diego Gelmírez, who sent clerics to study in France.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Skálholt
institutions.summary: School at the first Icelandic see, founded by Bishop Ísleifur Gissurarson, which trained Iceland's clergy and scholars for seven centuries. After the 1784 earthquakes it was moved to Reykjavík.
institutions.notes: Continued as the Latin school of Reykjavík (secondary level, out of scope).

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Hólar
institutions.summary: School at the northern Icelandic see founded by Jón Ögmundsson, who brought foreign masters to teach Latin and singing.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Lund
institutions.summary: School of the cathedral of Lund, archbishopric of all Scandinavia from 1103/04. It trained the Danish-Scanian clergy.
institutions.notes: Continued as a Lutheran Latin school (out of scope).

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Roskilde
institutions.summary: Danish cathedral school established in the early 11th century.
institutions.notes: Continued as a Latin school after 1536.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Ribe
institutions.summary: Cathedral school of Ribe, the oldest school in Denmark.
institutions.notes: Still exists as a gymnasium.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Nidaros
institutions.summary: Cathedral school founded with the archdiocese of Nidaros by Cardinal Nicholas Breakspear.
institutions.notes: Continued as a Latin school after the Reformation.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Esztergom
institutions.summary: School of the Hungarian primatial see founded by King Stephen I.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Veszprém
institutions.summary: Cathedral school teaching liberal arts and canon law, the most advanced in medieval Hungary.

institutions.name: Abbey School of Pannonhalma
institutions.summary: Benedictine abbey founded by Prince Géza and Stephen I, the oldest school in Hungary.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Gniezno
institutions.summary: School of the Polish metropolitan see established at the Congress of Gniezno (1000).

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Kraków
institutions.summary: Wawel cathedral school, attested by a library catalogue of 1110, which trained clergy before the founding of the university.

institutions.name: Cathedral School of Prague
institutions.summary: St Vitus cathedral school, where Adalbert taught.

events.title: Bardas founds the Magnaura school
events.desc: The Caesar Bardas organized salaried chairs of philosophy, geometry, astronomy and grammar in the Magnaura palace hall under Leo the Mathematician.

events.title: Revival under Constantine VII
events.desc: Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, on beginning his sole rule, appointed state-paid teachers of philosophy, rhetoric, geometry and astronomy and supported their students.

events.title: Superseded by Constantine IX's schools
events.desc: Imperial higher teaching was reorganized by Constantine IX Monomachos into new schools of law and philosophy, ending the Magnaura as a distinct institution.

events.title: Constantine IX founds the School of Philosophy
events.desc: Constantine IX Monomachos created the office of hypatos ton philosophon (consul of the philosophers), first held by Michael Psellos, to lead state-sponsored philosophical teaching.

events.title: Condemnation of John Italos
events.desc: The consul of philosophers John Italos was tried and anathematized for Neoplatonic teachings under Alexios I, curbing independent philosophical teaching in the capital.

events.title: Sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade
events.desc: The Latin conquest of April 1204 scattered the capital's teachers and libraries; higher learning continued in exile at Nicaea.

events.title: Restoration under Michael VIII
events.desc: After the recovery of Constantinople, Michael VIII Palaiologos had George Akropolites teach philosophy and mathematics at state expense in the capital.

events.title: Ottoman conquest of Constantinople
events.desc: The fall of the city on 29 May 1453 ended Byzantine imperial higher teaching; many scholars fled to Italy.

events.title: Novella founding the law school
events.desc: Constantine IX's novel established a salaried nomophylax (John Xiphilinos) to teach law, requiring advocates and notaries to obtain his certificate.

events.title: Fourth Crusade
events.desc: The sack of Constantinople ended whatever survived of the formal law school.

events.title: Alexios I organizes the patriarchal teachers
events.desc: An edict of Alexios I Komnenos reorganized the order of patriarchal didaskaloi (teachers of the Gospel, the Apostle and the Psalter) at Hagia Sophia.

events.title: Fourth Crusade sack
events.desc: The Latin sack of Constantinople and the flight of the patriarch to Nicaea broke up the patriarchal school.

events.title: Re-establishment by Gennadios Scholarios
events.desc: The first post-conquest patriarch, Gennadios II Scholarios, reopened the school with Matthaios Kamariotis as its master.

events.title: Aristotelian curriculum of Korydalleus
events.desc: Under Patriarch Cyril Loukaris, Theophilos Korydalleus reorganized teaching around Paduan neo-Aristotelianism, a curriculum that dominated Greek schools for over a century.

events.title: Endowment by Manolakis Kastorianos
events.desc: The furrier Manolakis of Kastoria endowed the school, restoring its finances and teaching.

events.title: Move to Xirokrini
events.desc: The school moved to new premises at Xirokrini on the Golden Horn, becoming known as the Patriarchal School of Xirokrini.

events.title: New building at the Phanar
events.desc: Construction began (1881-83) of the large red-brick building above the Patriarchate, funded by Georgios Zarifis, housing the Great School of the Nation.

events.title: Learning re-established in exile at Nicaea
events.desc: After the fall of Constantinople, scholars and the patriarchate gathered at the Laskarid court of Nicaea (capital from c. 1208), where court teaching was organized.

events.title: Schools of Theodore II Laskaris
events.desc: Theodore II Laskaris, Blemmydes' pupil, founded schools of grammar and rhetoric at Nicaea, including at the church of St Tryphon.

events.title: Restoration by Theodore Metochites
events.desc: Theodore Metochites rebuilt and endowed the Chora monastery and its library, where he and Gregoras taught.

events.title: Ottoman conquest
events.desc: The monastery and its library were dispersed at the fall of Constantinople; the church later became a mosque.

events.title: Plethon settles at Mistra
events.desc: Gemistos Plethon, exiled from Constantinople, settled at the Despotate court and began teaching Platonic philosophy.

events.title: Ottoman conquest of the Morea
events.desc: Mehmed II's conquest of the Despotate of the Morea ended the Mistra circle.

events.title: Makarios Kalogeras founds the school
events.desc: Makarios Kalogeras opened the school beside the Cave of the Apocalypse with patriarchal support.

events.title: Foundation at Vatopedi
events.desc: The academy opened in a building near Vatopedi with Neophytos Kafsokalyvitis as first head.

events.title: Directorship of Eugenios Voulgaris
events.desc: Voulgaris introduced Locke, Leibniz, Wolff and Newtonian physics; the school briefly drew around 200 students.

events.title: Departure of Voulgaris under conservative pressure
events.desc: Opposition from traditionalist monks forced Voulgaris to resign; the school declined.

events.title: Closure at the Greek Revolution
events.desc: The school closed when the War of Independence reached Mount Athos.

events.title: Revived at Karyes
events.desc: The academy was re-established at Karyes, administrative centre of the Holy Mountain.

events.title: Move to Karyes
events.desc: The revived school was seated at Karyes rather than Vatopedi.

events.title: Endowment by Emmanuel Gioumas
events.desc: The merchant Gioumas endowed a higher Greek school in Ioannina.

events.title: Foundation by the Maroutsis family
events.desc: The school opened with Eugenios Voulgaris as its first master.

events.title: Succeeded by the Kaplaneios School
events.desc: Financial difficulties closed the Maroutsaia; it was continued in the newly endowed Kaplaneios School.

events.title: Endowment by the Kaplanis brothers
events.desc: The Kaplaneios opened under Athanasios Psalidas, continuing the Maroutsaia.

events.title: Siege of Ioannina
events.desc: The school was destroyed when Ottoman forces besieged Ali Pasha in Ioannina (1820-22).

events.title: Foundation of the school
events.desc: The Orthodox community of Smyrna founded the school, with its first teacher Ierotheos Dendrinos.

events.title: British protection
events.desc: The school was placed under the protection of the British consulate, shielding it from Ottoman and ecclesiastical interference.

events.title: Athanasios Parios heads the school
events.desc: The community school of Chios was established as a higher school under Athanasios Parios.

events.title: Reorganization by Neophytos Vamvas
events.desc: Vamvas, a student of the Paris Enlightenment and friend of Korais, introduced sciences, a laboratory and a press.

events.title: Massacre of Chios
events.desc: Ottoman reprisals for the Chian uprising destroyed the school and killed or enslaved much of the population.

events.title: Foundation of the academy
events.desc: The community of Kydonies founded the academy, soon directed by Benjamin of Lesbos.

events.title: Burning of Kydonies
events.desc: The town and academy were destroyed by Ottoman forces in June 1821 at the start of the Greek Revolution.

events.title: Opening of the Academy
events.desc: The Ionian Academy opened in Corfu with Frederick North, 5th Earl of Guilford, as chancellor.

events.title: Guilford's death and decline
events.desc: After Guilford's death his library and endowment were withdrawn and the Academy was reduced in scope.

events.title: Abolished after union with Greece
events.desc: On the cession of the Ionian Islands to Greece the Academy was closed, the University of Athens becoming the national university.

events.title: Foundation of the Othonian University
events.desc: Founded by royal decree and opened on 3 May 1837 in the house of the architect Kleanthis in Plaka with four faculties.

events.title: Move to Hansen's building
events.desc: The university moved to the new neoclassical building by Christian Hansen on Panepistimiou Street.

events.title: Renamed National University
events.desc: After the overthrow of King Otto the Othonian University was renamed the National University.

events.title: Admission of women
events.desc: Ioanna Stefanopoli became the first woman admitted to study at the university.

events.title: Royal School of Arts opens
events.desc: The school opened as a Sunday school teaching architectural drawing and building crafts.

events.title: Higher technical school
events.desc: Reorganized as a higher school of industrial arts training civil and mechanical engineers.

events.title: Foundation by Germanos IV
events.desc: Patriarch Germanos IV opened the theological school in October 1844.

events.title: Opening of the Rizarios school
events.desc: The school opened with the Rizaris brothers' endowment.

events.title: Opening of the Velika škola
events.desc: The school opened in Belgrade on 13 September 1808 under the insurgent government of Karađorđe.

events.title: Collapse of the First Serbian Uprising
events.desc: The Ottoman reconquest of Belgrade ended the school.

events.title: Lyceum founded in Kragujevac
events.desc: Prince Miloš Obrenović's government founded the Lyceum with a philosophy course.

events.title: Move to Belgrade
events.desc: The Lyceum moved with the capital to Belgrade.

events.title: Reorganized as the Velika škola
events.desc: The Lyceum was reorganized as the Higher School with faculties of philosophy, law and engineering.

events.title: Higher Pedagogical Course opens
events.desc: Opened on 1 October 1888 with a history-philology course; Aleksandar Teodorov-Balan was first rector.

events.title: Faculty of law added
events.desc: Physics-mathematics (1889) and law faculties were added, completing the Higher School.

events.title: Opening in Bebek
events.desc: Hamlin opened the college in the buildings of the Bebek seminary.

events.title: Move to Rumeli Hisarı
events.desc: The college moved to its new campus above the Bosporus.

events.title: Opening of the college
events.desc: The college opened in December 1866 with Daniel Bliss as president.

events.title: Switch to English instruction
events.desc: Following the Darwin affair (Lewis affair), instruction changed from Arabic to English.

events.title: Jesuit college established in Beirut
events.desc: The Jesuits moved their seminary from Ghazir and opened the college in Beirut.

events.title: Pontifical powers
events.desc: Leo XIII granted the right to confer degrees in philosophy and theology.

events.title: French faculty of medicine
events.desc: A faculty of medicine was founded with French government support.

events.title: Foundation of the college
events.desc: Cyril V opened the clerical college in Cairo.

events.title: Alcuin joins the court
events.desc: Alcuin of York came to Charlemagne's court and took charge of teaching.

events.title: Aachen monastic legislation
events.desc: The Aachen reforms of Louis the Pious and Benedict of Aniane (816-817) restricted monastic schools to oblates, encouraging separate outer schools.

events.title: Division of the court after Louis the Pious
events.desc: With Louis the Pious's death and the partition of the empire, court teaching passed to the successor kingdoms.

events.title: Court school of Charles the Bald
events.desc: After Verdun, Charles the Bald maintained scholars at his court.

events.title: Death of Charles the Bald
events.desc: The court school declined after Charles's death.

events.title: Alfred gathers scholars
events.desc: Alfred recruited Asser, Grimbald and John the Old Saxon to his court.

events.title: Alfredian translation programme
events.desc: Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care announced that free-born youths should be taught to read English.

events.title: Bruno directs court teaching
events.desc: Bruno, Otto I's brother, became head of the royal chapel and court school.

events.title: Law teaching at the Pavian palace court
events.desc: Judges of the palace court began systematic teaching of Lombard law.

events.title: Expositio ad Librum Papiensem
events.desc: The Pavian jurists composed the Expositio, integrating Roman law.

events.title: Roman law teaching at Ravenna
events.desc: Roman law studies attested in Ravenna.

events.title: Alcuin becomes abbot of St Martin
events.desc: Charlemagne made Alcuin abbot of St Martin's, where he organized the school and scriptorium until his death in 804.

events.title: Viking sack of Tours
events.desc: Viking raiders burned Tours and the abbey of St Martin in November 853.

events.title: Condemnation of Berengar
events.desc: Berengar of Tours' symbolic Eucharistic teaching was condemned at the councils of Rome and Vercelli; Lanfranc of Bec led the attack on it.

events.title: Foundation of Fulda abbey
events.desc: Sturm founded the abbey of Fulda on 12 March 744 under Boniface's direction; a school is attested soon after.

events.title: Hrabanus Maurus becomes abbot
events.desc: Hrabanus Maurus, Alcuin's pupil and Fulda's master, was elected abbot and greatly expanded the library and school.

events.title: Gottschalk released from his oblation
events.desc: The Synod of Mainz freed Gottschalk from his monastic vows at Fulda against Hrabanus' wishes, beginning the predestination controversy.

events.title: Pirmin founds Reichenau
events.desc: The missionary bishop Pirmin founded the abbey on Reichenau island in 724.

events.title: Walafrid Strabo becomes abbot
events.desc: Walafrid Strabo, pupil of Hrabanus at Fulda and tutor to Charles the Bald, became abbot of Reichenau.

events.title: Otmar founds the abbey
events.desc: Otmar organized a Benedictine monastery at the hermitage of St Gallus in 719.

events.title: Hungarian raid
events.desc: Magyar raiders plundered St Gall; the library had been evacuated to Reichenau.

events.title: Fire at St Gall
events.desc: A fire started by a pupil destroyed much of the abbey.

events.title: Foundation of Corbie
events.desc: Queen Balthild founded the abbey c. 657-661.

events.title: Foundation of Corvey
events.desc: Monks from Corbie founded the daughter house of Corvey in Saxony.

events.title: Foundation of Corvey
events.desc: Monks of Corbie founded Corvey on the Weser (refounded at its final site in 822).

events.title: Lupus becomes abbot
events.desc: Charles the Bald made Lupus abbot of Ferrières in 840.

events.title: Haimo teaching at Saint-Germain
events.desc: Haimo of Auxerre was teaching at Saint-Germain by c. 840.

events.title: Leidrad restores the school
events.desc: Archbishop Leidrad reported to Charlemagne that he had founded schools of chant and of reading at Lyon.

events.title: Theodulf's capitulary
events.desc: Bishop Theodulf of Orléans ordered schools in his diocese and taught at the cathedral.

events.title: Succession by the law studium
events.desc: The schools developed into the studium of Orléans, recognized as a university in 1306.

events.title: Fulk restores the school
events.desc: Archbishop Fulk summoned Remigius of Auxerre and Hucbald of Saint-Amand to restore the cathedral school.

events.title: Gerbert becomes scholasticus
events.desc: Gerbert introduced a full quadrivium using the abacus and armillary spheres.

events.title: Odo of Cluny reforms Fleury
events.desc: Odo of Cluny reformed the abbey c. 930, inaugurating its intellectual revival.

events.title: Fulbert teaches at Chartres
events.desc: Fulbert, Gerbert's pupil, began teaching at the cathedral school c. 990.

events.title: Gregory VII on cathedral schools
events.desc: A Roman synod under Gregory VII (1078/1079) ordered bishops to maintain teaching of letters in their churches.

events.title: Third Lateran Council
events.desc: Canon 18 of Lateran III required every cathedral to maintain a master to teach clerics and poor scholars free of charge.

events.title: Fire at Chartres
events.desc: A fire destroyed most of the Romanesque cathedral and town; by then the school was being eclipsed by Paris.

events.title: Irish masters at Laon
events.desc: Martin Hiberniensis taught at Laon from c. 850.

events.title: Commune revolt
events.desc: The Laon communal uprising killed Bishop Gaudry and burned the cathedral.

events.title: William of Champeaux teaches at Notre-Dame
events.desc: William of Champeaux was master of the cathedral school c. 1100.

events.title: Absorption into the University
events.desc: Its masters formed the core of the universitas recognized by Philip Augustus in 1200.

events.title: William of Champeaux at St Victor
events.desc: William of Champeaux retired to the hermitage of St Victor and resumed teaching.

events.title: Royal endowment
events.desc: Louis VI founded and endowed the abbey of St Victor.

events.title: Overtaken by the University
events.desc: Teaching at St Victor declined as the mendicant and secular masters of the University dominated theology.

events.title: Abelard teaches on the hill
events.desc: Abelard set up his school on the Mont Sainte-Geneviève c. 1110.

events.title: Absorption into the University
events.desc: The arts masters of the Left Bank were absorbed into the University of Paris.

events.title: Lanfranc opens the school
events.desc: Lanfranc of Pavia opened a school at Bec c. 1045.

events.title: Sedulius Scottus at Liège
events.desc: Sedulius Scottus arrived at Liège c. 848-850.

events.title: Notger becomes bishop
events.desc: Bishop Notger reorganized the cathedral and its schools.

events.title: School of Gregory of Utrecht
events.desc: Gregory, Boniface's disciple, ran a school for missionaries at Utrecht.

events.title: Viking attack
events.desc: Vikings sacked Utrecht; the bishops withdrew until 918-925.

events.title: Bruno becomes archbishop
events.desc: Bruno became archbishop of Cologne and made its school a nursery of the imperial episcopate.

events.title: Thangmar teaching
events.desc: Thangmar taught at the cathedral school.

events.title: Foundation with the archdiocese
events.desc: Otto I's foundation of the archdiocese in 968 included a cathedral school.

events.title: School attested
events.desc: A cathedral school at Würzburg is attested around 1000.

events.title: Foundation with the diocese
events.desc: Henry II founded the diocese of Bamberg in 1007.

events.title: Theodore and Hadrian's school
events.desc: Theodore of Tarsus and Hadrian opened the school after arriving in 669-670.

events.title: Danish sack of Canterbury
events.desc: Danes sacked Canterbury and captured Archbishop Ælfheah.

events.title: Egbert's school
events.desc: Archbishop Egbert organized the school.

events.title: Viking capture of York
events.desc: The Great Heathen Army captured York, dispersing the school and library.

events.title: Æthelwold becomes bishop
events.desc: Æthelwold became bishop and replaced the canons with monks.

events.title: Foundation of Ramsey
events.desc: Oswald and Ealdorman Æthelwine founded Ramsey abbey.

events.title: Columba founds Iona
events.desc: Columba founded the monastery on Iona.

events.title: Viking massacre
events.desc: Vikings killed sixty-eight monks; the community moved to Kells.

events.title: School of Armagh
events.desc: The church of Armagh had an organized school by the 7th century.

events.title: Viking raids
events.desc: Vikings raided Armagh three times in one month.

events.title: High-king's lectorship
events.desc: Rory O'Connor endowed the lector of Armagh to teach students from Ireland and Scotland.

events.title: Ciarán founds Clonmacnoise
events.desc: St Ciarán founded the monastery.

events.title: Viking raids
events.desc: Vikings under Turgesius sacked Clonmacnoise.

events.title: Benedict founds Monte Cassino
events.desc: Benedict founded the monastery c. 529.

events.title: Saracen destruction
events.desc: Saracens destroyed the abbey; it was restored in 949.

events.title: Columbanus founds Bobbio
events.desc: Columbanus founded Bobbio.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I's capitulary created schools at Pavia, Ivrea, Turin, Cremona, Florence, Fermo, Verona, Vicenza and Cividale.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Ivrea as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Turin as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Cremona as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Florence as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Verona as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Vicenza as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Cividale as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Capitulary of Olona
events.desc: Lothar I named Fermo as a seat for one of the schools of Italy.

events.title: Gerbert studies at Vic
events.desc: Gerbert was brought to Catalonia by Count Borrell and studied under Atto of Vic.

events.title: Wilfred founds Ripoll
events.desc: Count Wilfred the Hairy founded Santa Maria de Ripoll.

events.title: Archbishop Raymond sponsors translations
events.desc: Archbishop Raymond (1125-1152) patronized translators.

events.title: Gelmírez organizes the school
events.desc: Bishop Diego Gelmírez organized masters of grammar and liberal arts.

events.title: Ísleifur's school
events.desc: Ísleifur Gissurarson, first bishop of Iceland, taught at Skálholt.

events.title: Lutheran Reformation
events.desc: The Reformation imposed by Denmark turned the school into a Lutheran Latin school.

events.title: South Iceland earthquakes
events.desc: Earthquakes destroyed most of Skálholt's buildings.

events.title: Transfer to Reykjavík
events.desc: The see and school were transferred to Reykjavík, ending the school at Skálholt.

events.title: Jón Ögmundsson founds the school
events.desc: Jón Ögmundsson, first bishop of Hólar, founded the school.

events.title: Lutheran Reformation
events.desc: After Jón Arason's execution in 1550, Hólar passed to Lutheran control.

events.title: Closure
events.desc: The school was closed and merged with the Reykjavík school.

events.title: Canute IV's charter
events.desc: Canute IV's gift charter for Lund (1085) mentions a school.

events.title: Danish Reformation
events.desc: The Reformation ended the Catholic chapter's control of the school.

events.title: School attested
events.desc: A cathedral school at Roskilde is attested in the early 11th century.

events.title: Danish Reformation
events.desc: The school passed to Lutheran control.

events.title: School attested
events.desc: A cathedral school is attested c. 1145.

events.title: Danish Reformation
events.desc: The school passed to Lutheran control.

events.title: Foundation with the archdiocese
events.desc: The archdiocese of Nidaros was established in 1152/53.

events.title: Norwegian Reformation
events.desc: The school passed to Lutheran control.

events.title: Foundation with the archbishopric
events.desc: Stephen I founded the archbishopric of Esztergom c. 1000.

events.title: Mongol invasion
events.desc: The Mongols sacked Esztergom.

events.title: School attested
events.desc: The school is attested c. 1200.

events.title: Sack by Péter Csák
events.desc: Péter Csák's troops destroyed the school and library.

events.title: Foundation of the abbey
events.desc: The abbey was founded in 996.

events.title: Foundation of the archbishopric
events.desc: The archbishopric was established in 1000.

events.title: Bohemian sack
events.desc: Bretislaus I sacked Gniezno.

events.title: School attested
events.desc: The cathedral school is attested c. 1100.

events.title: Fourth Lateran Council
events.desc: Canon 11 of Lateran IV reaffirmed the requirement of masters.

events.title: School attested
events.desc: The cathedral school is attested c. 1000.

events.title: Absorption into Charles University
events.desc: Teaching passed to the new university.

thinkers.name: Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher
thinkers.note: Studied under Leo and Photios; later apostle to the Slavs.

thinkers.name: Photios
thinkers.note: Teaching at the Magnaura is traditional but debated.

thinkers.name: Nikephoros Blemmydes
thinkers.note: Teacher of Akropolites and Theodore II.

thinkers.name: Methodios Anthrakites
thinkers.note: Pupil of Georgios Sougdouris; condemned by the Patriarchate 1723, then director before moving to the Epiphaneios school (1725).
